name: Rufus Brown's Boarding House

documented_range.note: DOCUMENTED IN FABRIC, USE, KEEPER AND POSITION, and absent from this dataset until now. Andreas describes a log house kept as a first-class boarding house by Mrs Rufus Brown, 'the first building in the rear of this store' - Peck's store at South Water and LaSalle. The range opens at the start of 1833, which is not a build date: what is documented is that the house was standing and keeping boarders in the town of 1833-34, and nothing follows it past 1835.

change_note: The building as this dataset can state it on the scene date. Where the sources give a size, a plan or a fabric, the record carries it; where they do not, the note says so attribute by attribute.

placement.position_note: THE RELATIVE POSITION IS DOCUMENTED AND THE ABSOLUTE ONE IS DERIVED FROM IT. 'The first building in the rear of this store' puts the boarding house immediately behind Peck's store, which this dataset places at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle. This record sits directly south of peck_store's footprint, on the same lot line, facing north onto the same yard. WHAT IS NOT DOCUMENTED: the distance behind the store, the orientation, and whether 'in the rear' means the same lot or the next one. The 20 m working georeference uncertainty of the whole dataset applies on top.
placement.symbolic_location: South Division, local ENU E 428 N -30

footprint.note: PLACEHOLDER - NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED. 24 x 40 ft is a log boarding house with a hall and two rooms below and a sleeping loft above, which is the smallest thing that answers 'a first-class boarding house' with a keeper, her household and paying boarders in it. Every number is invented.

function.note: THE HIGHEST-VALUE SINGLE BUILDING PHASE ONE FOUND, and the reason is that boarding houses bridge the gap between 3,265 people and 398 dwellings. Andreas on the houses of 1834: they 'were always full; and full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides', with emigrants living in their covered wagons outside. persons.name: Rufus Brown
persons.note: One of the nine village citizens among the twenty-six founding members of the First Presbyterian Church on 26 June 1833, and a signatory of the 1832 militia agreement submitting to Gholson Kercheval as captain 'until all apprehension of danger from the Indians may have subsided'.

persons.name: Mrs Rufus Brown
persons.note: A WOMAN NAMED ONLY BY HER HUSBAND'S NAME AND DOCUMENTED AS THE PROPRIETOR OF A BUSINESS, which is a combination this literature produces constantly and this schema has to be able to carry. Two women named Brown are among the nine village citizens founding the First Presbyterian Church in June 1833 - 'Mrs. Elizabeth Brown' and 'Mrs. Cynthia Brown' - and one of them may be this woman. The record does not choose: identifying her with either would manufacture a forename out of a surname.

residents.research_note: THE ONE HOUSEHOLD IN THIS PARCEL WHOSE BUILDING IS DOCUMENTED, POSITIONED AND ABSENT FROM THE MODEL. Andreas gives the fabric (log), the use (first-class boarding house), the keeper (Mrs Rufus Brown) and the position (immediately behind Peck's store at South Water and LaSalle) - which is more than several buildings already standing in this scene have. A structure record for it is the highest-value single piece of work this parcel has generated. WHY BOARDING HOUSES MATTER OUT OF ALL PROPORTION TO THEIR NUMBER: Andreas says the hotels and boarding houses of 1834 'were always full; and full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides', with emigrants living in their covered wagons outside. The gap between 3,265 people and the dwellings this dataset can name is bridged largely by buildings like this one.
